bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Product-cycle dependence — domestic volumes fall when the launch/refresh cadence lags competitors — The Company states plainly that 'domestic sales noted a decline due to lower product enhancement activity compared to competitors', with domestic volumes down 2.3% to 584,906 units in FY 26 even as the industry PV segment grew 7.9% to a record 46,43,439 units. This is a self-diagnosed, company-specific loss of share, not a market problem, and it makes FY 27 volumes contingent on the two all-new SUV nameplates the Company has committed to launch.
- Model and segment concentration — SUVs, and CRETA in particular, carry the domestic mix — SUVs were 68.3% of FY 26 domestic sales (410,199 units in FY 25 falling to 399,569 in FY 26), and a single nameplate, CRETA, accounted for 2,01,921 units. Hatchbacks fell to 18.4% of the mix from 19.7%. A refresh miss, a regulatory change or a competitive launch against CRETA or the SUV segment would hit a disproportionate share of domestic revenue.
- Channel concentration on a dealer network the Company does not own — BRSR Principle 1 'Open-ness of business' discloses that sales to dealers/distributors were 99.99% of total sales in FY 2025-26 (99.5% in FY 2024-25), spread over 786 total dealers (658 main 3S dealers plus 128 urban compact 1S), with the top 10 dealers at 14.0% of sales to dealers. Essentially all revenue passes through an independent franchise channel, so dealer health, inventory discipline and the 89 net additions per year are structural exposures rather than operating details.
- Related-party dependence in the supply chain — Purchases from related parties were 29.52% of total purchases in FY 2025-26 (32.66% in FY 2024-25) and sales to related parties 7.29% of total sales. The related-party roster runs to more than forty Hyundai-group entities, including Mobis India Ltd — the single material arm's-length contract disclosed in Form AOC-2 — plus Hyundai Transys, Hyundai Wia, Hyundai Autoever and HEC India. Roughly three rupees in ten of input cost is set inside the group, so HMIL's cost line is not fully arm's-length-determined in practice even where it is arm's-length in form.
- Export exposure to geopolitics, tariffs and freight — a quarter of turnover — Exports were 25.25% of turnover per the BRSR (the Board's Report states 25.56% of revenue and the Export spotlight states 25%; the AR does not reconcile the three). Management flags the West Asia conflict disrupting energy supply routes and raising fuel and logistics costs, US automotive tariff measures and sector-specific restrictions injecting uncertainty into global trade flows, and per FADA over 53% of dealers reporting some level of dispatch or supply disruption linked to the conflict. Export markets named (Latin America, Africa, Asia-Pacific, Middle East) are largely emerging economies exposed to energy-import inflation.
- Powertrain transition risk cutting both ways — and a shrinking EV capital commitment — Industry EV passenger vehicle volumes grew 93.9% in FY 26 and EV share of PV rose to 3.4% from 1.9%, while globally electrification momentum has 'softened in certain markets due to affordability concerns, infrastructure gaps and evolving subsidy regimes, leading to a more balanced shift towards hybrids'. Against that, HMIL's own EV-related capex fell to 4% of total capital expenditure in FY 2025-26 from 10% in FY 2024-25, and EV-related R&D to 30% from 38%. Higher fuel prices are also flagged as accelerating the shift toward CNG and EVs (around 36.5% of dealers say fuel costs are affecting buyer sentiment), so the Company is exposed to both an EV transition that arrives faster than its spend and one that stalls after it commits.
- Manufacturing and geographic concentration, now partially mitigated — Until October 2025 essentially all production sat at the Chennai complex (Plant 1 and Plant 2 being assembly lines within one factory, 8,24,000 units of installed capacity). The Pune (Talegaon) plant is explicitly justified as improving 'supply-chain resilience by diversifying HMIL's manufacturing footprint beyond a single region', which is management's own acknowledgement that single-site concentration was a structural risk. Pune itself is a new, single-model, ramping operation (64,830 units produced in FY 26) and therefore carries execution risk of its own.
- Enterprise risk framework names financial, operational, sectoral, sustainability, information and cyber-security risk — but no MD&A 'Risks & Concerns' section was disclosed in the routed text — The Board's Report states that a Risk Management Committee exists under Regulation 21 of SEBI LODR and that a Risk Management Policy was adopted at the board meeting of 12th June 2024 covering 'financial, operational, sectoral, sustainability, information, cyber security risks, or any other risk as may be determined by the Risk Management Committee', and it then refers the reader to the MD&A for details. IMPORTANT STATED-ABSENCE FINDING: no MD&A 'Risks and Concerns' section, no BRSR 'material responsible business conduct issues' risk-and-mitigation table, and no enumerated risk-factor list appears anywhere in the routed text — the cross-reference points to material that was not delivered in this bundle. The risks above are therefore reconstructed from concentration and outlook disclosures rather than read off a company risk register.
- Workforce structure and attrition — a largely contract shopfloor, rising employee churn and near-zero female representation among workers — Of 12,733 workers, 10,539 (82.8%) are 'other than permanent' against 2,194 permanent, i.e. the shopfloor is predominantly non-permanent, and the Board's Report acknowledges an Employees Union. Permanent-employee turnover rose to 7.94% in FY 26 from 5% in FY 25, with female employee turnover at 17.13% against 7.2% for males. Women are 7.1% of employees, 25% of the Board and 0% of the five Key Managerial Personnel, and there are zero permanent female workers. Employee LTIFR also rose to 0.11 from 0.09 per million person-hours.

outlook.body: HMIL's expansion story in FY 26 is the operationalisation of the Talegaon (Pune) plant. The facility was acquired from General Motors in August 2023 as a strategic brownfield acquisition, which the Company says let it accelerate capacity expansion through a capital-efficient route while significantly reducing the execution timelines associated with a greenfield project. Over FY 25 and FY 26 the plant underwent extensive revitalization and modernization aligned with Hyundai's latest global manufacturing standards, with the transformation completed within 19 months. Passenger vehicle production commenced in October 2025 and the plant is being ramped up in a phased manner; it currently adds 1,70,000 units to annual production capacity, with a stated total capacity of 3,20,000 units in phases by 2030. The plant is conceptualised as a flexible facility capable of producing both ICE vehicles and EVs on the same production lines, and it incorporates Industry 4.0 technology — advanced robotics across welding, painting and assembly, AI-enabled real-time quality inspection, machine-learning predictive maintenance, IoT-enabled equipment and digitally connected shopfloor systems. Within the first month of operations it transitioned to two-shift production; it recorded zero field complaints in its first 100 days, an exceptionally low warranty claim rate and over 16 million accident-free man-hours, and produced 64,830 units in FY 26 (production, not capacity). Strategically located in western India, Pune strengthens logistics and export capability through proximity to Mumbai ports and the Maharashtra/Gujarat component clusters and diversifies HMIL's manufacturing footprint beyond a single region. The Chennai plant remains the cornerstone of operations with an installed annual capacity of 8,24,000 units, and with Pune added the Company's total installed capacity has reached approximately 1 million units per annum. HMIL currently manufactures 15 passenger vehicle models across 450+ variants through a flexible, integrated manufacturing setup. On the composition of spend, the BRSR (Principle 2, Essential Indicator 1) states that EV-related capex was 4% of total capital expenditure in FY 2025-26 versus 10% in FY 2024-25, described as covering 'EV Cars, Battery Assembly Plant, Plant Expansion, Charging Station', while EV-related R&D was 30% of total R&D in FY 2025-26 versus 38% in FY 2024-25 — i.e. the EV share of the capital programme fell sharply year on year. || NAMED DISCLOSURE DEFECT — capital commitments figures NOT extracted: the '=== NAMED DISCLOSURE — CAPITAL COMMITMENTS ===' block supplied with this bundle carries no readable column dates (the header reads only 'As at | Year ended', with no year against either column) and no unit line (no 'Rs Million / Rs Lakhs / Rs Crore' statement anywhere in the block). Per the extraction rules the figures are therefore omitted rather than guessed, and capex_disclosed is returned empty. The block is reproduced verbatim here: '[page 159] As at | Year ended / Estimated amount of contracts remaining to be executed on capital account and not provided for / 11,122.35 / 12,045.54 / [page 193] As at | Year ended / (a) Estimated amount of contracts remaining to be executed on capital account and not provided for / 11,210.47 / 12,114.28'. Note also that the block prints two DIFFERENT pairs of figures for the same line item from two different pages (page 159 and page 193, presumably standalone and consolidated, though neither is labelled), which is a second reason the rows are not usable as stated. || SCOPE NOTE — the routed 'MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION & ANALYSIS' section of this bundle does not contain MD&A at all; it contains Annexure 'D' CSR impact-assessment write-ups (Art for Hope, clean water in Madhya Pradesh, rural sports, ITI support, Assam disaster management) and contributed no capex or capacity content. The 'CHAIRMAN / MD MESSAGE' section is likewise not the MD's letter but the manufacturing-quality and 'Pune plant: Manufacturing redefined' spotlight spreads — which is where all the Pune capex narrative above actually came from. || BACK-FILL FROM SIBLING BUNDLE (profile.txt, MD & CEO's statement): the MD states 'The current capacity at Pune is 1,70,000 units and we plan to scale it up to 3,20,000 in phases', a callout of '9,94,000 units — Total production capacity at present after Pune plant commissioning', investments of over ₹ 4,07,000 million in India since inception, and planned investments of ₹ 4,50,000 million over FY 26 – FY 30 announced at the Investor Day. Those rupee amounts are narrative statements, not named disclosures, so they are recorded as commitments rather than in capex_disclosed.

outlook.body:
- Global economy: growth broadly sustained at around 3.5% in 2025 (IMF July 2026 WEO Update), supported by accommodative financial conditions, policy support and technology-led investment; outlook cautiously moderated, with growth expected to ease to around 3.0% in 2026.
- Global inflation rose from 4.1% in 2025 to around 4.4% in 2026 on West Asia conflict-driven energy and logistics costs; expected to moderate gradually to 3.7% by 2027 assuming easing commodity prices.
- India macro: real GDP growth estimated at 7.7% in FY 26 (PIB) versus 7.1% in FY 25, led by secondary and tertiary sectors each expanding above 9%; IMF projects India real GDP growth of 6.4% for FY 27 and 6.7% for FY 28.
- GST 2.0 rate rationalization (simplified two-slab structure of 5% and 18%) was a key catalyst — described by the CFO as a strong growth catalyst from September that improved affordability and household disposable income; supported by income tax rationalization, multiple repo rate cuts and benign inflation of 2.1% for much of the year.
- Indian auto industry: FY 26 was a milestone year with all major segments recording their highest annual sales in seven years; SIAM total industry production of 34.7 million units.
- Passenger vehicles: record domestic sales of 46,43,439 units in FY 26, +7.9% YoY, with a highest-ever quarterly 13,16,282 units in Q4 on festive demand and improved retail conversions; drivers cited are improved affordability, tax rationalization, lower financing costs and sustained preference for utility vehicles and feature-rich models.
- Electrification: overall EV passenger vehicle growth of 93.9% (EV contribution to PV rising to 3.4% / 157,514 units in FY 26 from 1.9% / 81,226 units in FY 25); electric passenger vehicle registrations grew over 94%. Policy support from PLI-Auto, PLI for ACC battery storage, PM E-DRIVE, PM-eBus Sewa and SPMEPCI.
- Exports as a structural growth lever: India PV (4-wheeler) exports at a record 9,05,200 units, +17.5%, on steady demand from the Middle East, Africa and Latin America.
- Global auto: light vehicle sales of approximately 91.7 million units in 2025, surpassing pre-pandemic levels for the first time; projected at 91.86 million units in 2026 (S&P Global Mobility) — marginal growth, with production expected to moderate in 2026 amid trade policy uncertainty including US automotive tariffs.
- Softening electrification momentum in certain markets on affordability, infrastructure gaps and evolving subsidy regimes, leading to a more balanced shift towards hybrids and alternative powertrains — a driver behind HMIL's hybrid-ready architectures.
- Structural transformation through digitalization and software-defined vehicles, enabling new revenue streams via connected services and over-the-air upgrades.
- Supply chain risk, particularly in semiconductors and critical minerals, remains a key challenge for global manufacturers.
- Company-specific FY 26 drivers per the CFO: commissioning of the Pune plant coincided with the GST-driven demand improvement and the product launch cycle kicking in, collectively supporting HMIL's growth trajectory.
- Export business delivered 21.43% YoY revenue growth (CFO's statement); export destinations increased from over 60 countries in FY 25 to more than 70 countries in FY 26; VERNA and Grand i10 anchored export volumes, with strong demand from Latin America, Africa and Asia-Pacific.
- Mix driver: SUVs contributed ~68% of domestic sales in FY 26, significantly ahead of industry trends, led by CRETA.
- BACK-FILLED FROM SIBLING BUNDLE (profile.txt, MD&A 'Outlook' and 'Key Challenges' pages, routed there rather than here): Indian auto industry expected to sustain growth in FY 27 at a more moderate pace per ICRA — passenger vehicles projected to grow 4–6% and commercial vehicles 4–6%; medium-term shape set by premiumization, alternative powertrain adoption and rising EV penetration.
- BACK-FILLED FROM SIBLING BUNDLE (profile.txt): FY 27 challenges flagged — West Asia geopolitical tension with over 53% of dealers reporting dispatch/supply disruption (FADA), risk of higher fuel prices with around 36.5% of dealers saying fuel costs are affecting buyer sentiment and accelerating the shift toward CNG and EVs, and an expected phase of demand normalization after a strong year-end.
- BACK-FILLED FROM SIBLING BUNDLE (profile.txt, Corporate Overview 'Operational Performance'): HMIL's domestic sales declined in FY 26 due to lower product enhancement activity compared to competitors, while export sales volume grew around 16.4% — the key stated volume-mix driver of the year.
- Data caution: the AR states HMIL's FY 26 export contribution three different ways — 25% (Export spotlight callout), 25.56% of revenue (Board's Report) and 25.25% of turnover (BRSR). Reproduced as printed; not reconciled by the Company.
- Value-engineering margin lever: R&D/HMIE cost convention activities (CCW events, VAVE Convention, VE Pitstop) delivered cost reduction of ~₹ 39.3 Crore from 55 suggestions in CY 2025, with continued focus on localization and material change.
- No order book, order-inflow, booking or backlog disclosure appears anywhere in the routed strategy_outlook text — a stated absence rather than an omission. The Company is a passenger-vehicle OEM selling through a dealer network; the nearest forward-visibility disclosures it gives are the FY 27 launch plan (two all-new SUV nameplates), the plan to export the All-New VENUE to over 35 countries, and the phased Pune capacity ramp-up.

drhp.business: HMIL manufactures and sells passenger cars in India and for export, with a diversified portfolio spanning hatchbacks, sedans, SUVs and electric vehicles, and also sells vehicle parts and accessories such as engines, transmissions and other parts. It serves retail buyers of new and pre-owned cars, fleet operators and institutional clients through an authorised dealer network across India and through direct-to-customer (D2C) platforms, plus after-sales service, genuine parts and technical support via authorised service centres. As a subsidiary of Hyundai Motor Company, South Korea, it combines advanced mobility technologies, high localization and sustainable manufacturing; per the BRSR, manufacture of passenger cars accounts for 88.05% of turnover and sale of vehicle parts and accessories 4.92%.

drhp.expansion: HMIL's expansion story in FY 26 is the operationalisation of the Talegaon (Pune) plant. The facility was acquired from General Motors in August 2023 as a strategic brownfield acquisition, which the Company says let it accelerate capacity expansion through a capital-efficient route while significantly reducing the execution timelines associated with a greenfield project. Over FY 25 and FY 26 the plant underwent extensive revitalization and modernization aligned with Hyundai's latest global manufacturing standards, with the transformation completed within 19 months. Passenger vehicle production commenced in October 2025 and the plant is being ramped up in a phased manner; it currently adds 1,70,000 units to annual production capacity, with a stated total capacity of 3,20,000 units in phases by 2030. The plant is conceptualised as a flexible facility capable of producing both ICE vehicles and EVs on the same production lines, and it incorporates Industry 4.0 technology — advanced robotics across welding, painting and assembly, AI-enabled real-time quality inspection, machine-learning predictive maintenance, IoT-enabled equipment and digitally connected shopfloor systems. Within the first month of operations it transitioned to two-shift production; it recorded zero field complaints in its first 100 days, an exceptionally low warranty claim rate and over 16 million accident-free man-hours, and produced 64,830 units in FY 26 (production, not capacity). Strategically located in western India, Pune strengthens logistics and export capability through proximity to Mumbai ports and the Maharashtra/Gujarat component clusters and diversifies HMIL's manufacturing footprint beyond a single region. The Chennai plant remains the cornerstone of operations with an installed annual capacity of 8,24,000 units, and with Pune added the Company's total installed capacity has reached approximately 1 million units per annum. HMIL currently manufactures 15 passenger vehicle models across 450+ variants through a flexible, integrated manufacturing setup. On the composition of spend, the BRSR (Principle 2, Essential Indicator 1) states that EV-related capex was 4% of total capital expenditure in FY 2025-26 versus 10% in FY 2024-25, described as covering 'EV Cars, Battery Assembly Plant, Plant Expansion, Charging Station', while EV-related R&D was 30% of total R&D in FY 2025-26 versus 38% in FY 2024-25 — i.e. the EV share of the capital programme fell sharply year on year. || NAMED DISCLOSURE DEFECT — capital commitments figures NOT extracted: the '=== NAMED DISCLOSURE — CAPITAL COMMITMENTS ===' block supplied with this bundle carries no readable column dates (the header reads only 'As at | Year ended', with no year against either column) and no unit line (no 'Rs Million / Rs Lakhs / Rs Crore' statement anywhere in the block). risks.note: The Company states plainly that 'domestic sales noted a decline due to lower product enhancement activity compared to competitors', with domestic volumes down 2.3% to 584,906 units in FY 26 even as the industry PV segment grew 7.9% to a record 46,43,439 units. This is a self-diagnosed, company-specific loss of share, not a market problem, and it makes FY 27 volumes contingent on the two all-new SUV nameplates the Company has committed to launch.
risks.risk: Product-cycle dependence — domestic volumes fall when the launch/refresh cadence lags competitors

risks.note: SUVs were 68.3% of FY 26 domestic sales (410,199 units in FY 25 falling to 399,569 in FY 26), and a single nameplate, CRETA, accounted for 2,01,921 units. Hatchbacks fell to 18.4% of the mix from 19.7%. A refresh miss, a regulatory change or a competitive launch against CRETA or the SUV segment would hit a disproportionate share of domestic revenue.
risks.risk: Model and segment concentration — SUVs, and CRETA in particular, carry the domestic mix

risks.note: BRSR Principle 1 'Open-ness of business' discloses that sales to dealers/distributors were 99.99% of total sales in FY 2025-26 (99.5% in FY 2024-25), spread over 786 total dealers (658 main 3S dealers plus 128 urban compact 1S), with the top 10 dealers at 14.0% of sales to dealers. Essentially all revenue passes through an independent franchise channel, so dealer health, inventory discipline and the 89 net additions per year are structural exposures rather than operating details.
risks.risk: Channel concentration on a dealer network the Company does not own

risks.note: Purchases from related parties were 29.52% of total purchases in FY 2025-26 (32.66% in FY 2024-25) and sales to related parties 7.29% of total sales. The related-party roster runs to more than forty Hyundai-group entities, including Mobis India Ltd — the single material arm's-length contract disclosed in Form AOC-2 — plus Hyundai Transys, Hyundai Wia, Hyundai Autoever and HEC India. Roughly three rupees in ten of input cost is set inside the group, so HMIL's cost line is not fully arm's-length-determined in practice even where it is arm's-length in form.
risks.risk: Related-party dependence in the supply chain

risks.note: Exports were 25.25% of turnover per the BRSR (the Board's Report states 25.56% of revenue and the Export spotlight states 25%; the AR does not reconcile the three). Management flags the West Asia conflict disrupting energy supply routes and raising fuel and logistics costs, US automotive tariff measures and sector-specific restrictions injecting uncertainty into global trade flows, and per FADA over 53% of dealers reporting some level of dispatch or supply disruption linked to the conflict. Export markets named (Latin America, Africa, Asia-Pacific, Middle East) are largely emerging economies exposed to energy-import inflation.
risks.risk: Export exposure to geopolitics, tariffs and freight — a quarter of turnover

risks.note: Industry EV passenger vehicle volumes grew 93.9% in FY 26 and EV share of PV rose to 3.4% from 1.9%, while globally electrification momentum has 'softened in certain markets due to affordability concerns, infrastructure gaps and evolving subsidy regimes, leading to a more balanced shift towards hybrids'. Against that, HMIL's own EV-related capex fell to 4% of total capital expenditure in FY 2025-26 from 10% in FY 2024-25, and EV-related R&D to 30% from 38%. Higher fuel prices are also flagged as accelerating the shift toward CNG and EVs (around 36.5% of dealers say fuel costs are affecting buyer sentiment), so the Company is exposed to both an EV transition that arrives faster than its spend and one that stalls after it commits.
risks.risk: Powertrain transition risk cutting both ways — and a shrinking EV capital commitment

risks.note: Until October 2025 essentially all production sat at the Chennai complex (Plant 1 and Plant 2 being assembly lines within one factory, 8,24,000 units of installed capacity). The Pune (Talegaon) plant is explicitly justified as improving 'supply-chain resilience by diversifying HMIL's manufacturing footprint beyond a single region', which is management's own acknowledgement that single-site concentration was a structural risk. Pune itself is a new, single-model, ramping operation (64,830 units produced in FY 26) and therefore carries execution risk of its own.
risks.risk: Manufacturing and geographic concentration, now partially mitigated

risks.note: The Board's Report states that a Risk Management Committee exists under Regulation 21 of SEBI LODR and that a Risk Management Policy was adopted at the board meeting of 12th June 2024 covering 'financial, operational, sectoral, sustainability, information, cyber security risks, or any other risk as may be determined by the Risk Management Committee', and it then refers the reader to the MD&A for details. risks.note: Of 12,733 workers, 10,539 (82.8%) are 'other than permanent' against 2,194 permanent, i.e. the shopfloor is predominantly non-permanent, and the Board's Report acknowledges an Employees Union. Permanent-employee turnover rose to 7.94% in FY 26 from 5% in FY 25, with female employee turnover at 17.13% against 7.2% for males. Women are 7.1% of employees, 25% of the Board and 0% of the five Key Managerial Personnel, and there are zero permanent female workers. Employee LTIFR also rose to 0.11 from 0.09 per million person-hours.
risks.risk: Workforce structure and attrition — a largely contract shopfloor, rising employee churn and near-zero female representation among workers

summary.oneLiner: Hyundai Motor India Limited (HMIL) is one of India's leading passenger vehicle manufacturers and a key pillar of the Hyundai Group's global growth strategy, anchored in the philosophy of 'Progress for Humanity'.
summary.business: HMIL manufactures and sells passenger cars in India and for export, with a diversified portfolio spanning hatchbacks, sedans, SUVs and electric vehicles, and also sells vehicle parts and accessories such as engines, transmissions and other parts. It serves retail buyers of new and pre-owned cars, fleet operators and institutional clients through an authorised dealer network across India and through direct-to-customer (D2C) platforms, plus after-sales service, genuine parts and technical support via authorised service centres. As a subsidiary of Hyundai Motor Company, South Korea, it combines advanced mobility technologies, high localization and sustainable manufacturing; per the BRSR, manufacture of passenger cars accounts for 88.05% of turnover and sale of vehicle parts and accessories 4.92%.

currentContext.expansion: HMIL's expansion story in FY 26 is the operationalisation of the Talegaon (Pune) plant. The facility was acquired from General Motors in August 2023 as a strategic brownfield acquisition, which the Company says let it accelerate capacity expansion through a capital-efficient route while significantly reducing the execution timelines associated with a greenfield project. Over FY 25 and FY 26 the plant underwent extensive revitalization and modernization aligned with Hyundai's latest global manufacturing standards, with the transformation completed within 19 months. Passenger vehicle production commenced in October 2025 and the plant is being ramped up in a phased manner; it currently adds 1,70,000 units to annual production capacity, with a stated total capacity of 3,20,000 units in phases by 2030. The plant is conceptualised as a flexible facility capable of producing both ICE vehicles and EVs on the same production lines, and it incorporates Industry 4.0 technology — advanced robotics across welding, painting and assembly, AI-enabled real-time quality inspection, machine-learning predictive maintenance, IoT-enabled equipment and digitally connected shopfloor systems. Within the first month of operations it transitioned to two-shift production; it recorded zero field complaints in its first 100 days, an exceptionally low warranty claim rate and over 16 million accident-free man-hours, and produced 64,830 units in FY 26 (production, not capacity). Strategically located in western India, Pune strengthens logistics and export capability through proximity to Mumbai ports and the Maharashtra/Gujarat component clusters and diversifies HMIL's manufacturing footprint beyond a single region. The Chennai plant remains the cornerstone of operations with an installed annual capacity of 8,24,000 units, and with Pune added the Company's total installed capacity has reached approximately 1 million units per annum. HMIL currently manufactures 15 passenger vehicle models across 450+ variants through a flexible, integrated manufacturing setup. risks.risk: Product-cycle dependence — domestic volumes fall when the launch/refresh cadence lags competitors
risks.note: The Company states plainly that 'domestic sales noted a decline due to lower product enhancement activity compared to competitors', with domestic volumes down 2.3% to 584,906 units in FY 26 even as the industry PV segment grew 7.9% to a record 46,43,439 units. This is a self-diagnosed, company-specific loss of share, not a market problem, and it makes FY 27 volumes contingent on the two all-new SUV nameplates the Company has committed to launch.

risks.risk: Model and segment concentration — SUVs, and CRETA in particular, carry the domestic mix
risks.note: SUVs were 68.3% of FY 26 domestic sales (410,199 units in FY 25 falling to 399,569 in FY 26), and a single nameplate, CRETA, accounted for 2,01,921 units. Hatchbacks fell to 18.4% of the mix from 19.7%. A refresh miss, a regulatory change or a competitive launch against CRETA or the SUV segment would hit a disproportionate share of domestic revenue.

risks.risk: Channel concentration on a dealer network the Company does not own
risks.note: BRSR Principle 1 'Open-ness of business' discloses that sales to dealers/distributors were 99.99% of total sales in FY 2025-26 (99.5% in FY 2024-25), spread over 786 total dealers (658 main 3S dealers plus 128 urban compact 1S), with the top 10 dealers at 14.0% of sales to dealers. Essentially all revenue passes through an independent franchise channel, so dealer health, inventory discipline and the 89 net additions per year are structural exposures rather than operating details.

risks.risk: Related-party dependence in the supply chain
risks.note: Purchases from related parties were 29.52% of total purchases in FY 2025-26 (32.66% in FY 2024-25) and sales to related parties 7.29% of total sales. The related-party roster runs to more than forty Hyundai-group entities, including Mobis India Ltd — the single material arm's-length contract disclosed in Form AOC-2 — plus Hyundai Transys, Hyundai Wia, Hyundai Autoever and HEC India. Roughly three rupees in ten of input cost is set inside the group, so HMIL's cost line is not fully arm's-length-determined in practice even where it is arm's-length in form.

risks.risk: Export exposure to geopolitics, tariffs and freight — a quarter of turnover
risks.note: Exports were 25.25% of turnover per the BRSR (the Board's Report states 25.56% of revenue and the Export spotlight states 25%; the AR does not reconcile the three). Management flags the West Asia conflict disrupting energy supply routes and raising fuel and logistics costs, US automotive tariff measures and sector-specific restrictions injecting uncertainty into global trade flows, and per FADA over 53% of dealers reporting some level of dispatch or supply disruption linked to the conflict. Export markets named (Latin America, Africa, Asia-Pacific, Middle East) are largely emerging economies exposed to energy-import inflation.

risks.risk: Powertrain transition risk cutting both ways — and a shrinking EV capital commitment
risks.note: Industry EV passenger vehicle volumes grew 93.9% in FY 26 and EV share of PV rose to 3.4% from 1.9%, while globally electrification momentum has 'softened in certain markets due to affordability concerns, infrastructure gaps and evolving subsidy regimes, leading to a more balanced shift towards hybrids'. Against that, HMIL's own EV-related capex fell to 4% of total capital expenditure in FY 2025-26 from 10% in FY 2024-25, and EV-related R&D to 30% from 38%. Higher fuel prices are also flagged as accelerating the shift toward CNG and EVs (around 36.5% of dealers say fuel costs are affecting buyer sentiment), so the Company is exposed to both an EV transition that arrives faster than its spend and one that stalls after it commits.

risks.risk: Manufacturing and geographic concentration, now partially mitigated
risks.note: Until October 2025 essentially all production sat at the Chennai complex (Plant 1 and Plant 2 being assembly lines within one factory, 8,24,000 units of installed capacity). The Pune (Talegaon) plant is explicitly justified as improving 'supply-chain resilience by diversifying HMIL's manufacturing footprint beyond a single region', which is management's own acknowledgement that single-site concentration was a structural risk. Pune itself is a new, single-model, ramping operation (64,830 units produced in FY 26) and therefore carries execution risk of its own.

risks.risk: Enterprise risk framework names financial, operational, sectoral, sustainability, information and cyber-security risk — but no MD&A 'Risks & Concerns' section was disclosed in the routed text
risks.note: The Board's Report states that a Risk Management Committee exists under Regulation 21 of SEBI LODR and that a Risk Management Policy was adopted at the board meeting of 12th June 2024 covering 'financial, operational, sectoral, sustainability, information, cyber security risks, or any other risk as may be determined by the Risk Management Committee', and it then refers the reader to the MD&A for details. IMPORTANT STATED-ABSENCE FINDING: no MD&A 'Risks and Concerns' section, no BRSR 'material responsible business conduct issues' risk-and-mitigation table, and no enumerated risk-factor list appears anywhere in the routed text — the cross-reference points to material that was not delivered in this bundle. The risks above are therefore reconstructed from concentration and outlook disclosures rather than read off a company risk register.

risks.risk: Workforce structure and attrition — a largely contract shopfloor, rising employee churn and near-zero female representation among workers
risks.note: Of 12,733 workers, 10,539 (82.8%) are 'other than permanent' against 2,194 permanent, i.e. the shopfloor is predominantly non-permanent, and the Board's Report acknowledges an Employees Union. Permanent-employee turnover rose to 7.94% in FY 26 from 5% in FY 25, with female employee turnover at 17.13% against 7.2% for males. Women are 7.1% of employees, 25% of the Board and 0% of the five Key Managerial Personnel, and there are zero permanent female workers. Employee LTIFR also rose to 0.11 from 0.09 per million person-hours.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Hyundai Motor India Limited (HMIL) is one of India's leading passenger vehicle manufacturers and a key pillar of the Hyundai Group's global growth strategy, anchored in the philosophy of 'Progress for Humanity'.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: HMIL manufactures and sells passenger cars in India and for export, with a diversified portfolio spanning hatchbacks, sedans, SUVs and electric vehicles, and also sells vehicle parts and accessories such as engines, transmissions and other parts. It serves retail buyers of new and pre-owned cars, fleet operators and institutional clients through an authorised dealer network across India and through direct-to-customer (D2C) platforms, plus after-sales service, genuine parts and technical support via authorised service centres. As a subsidiary of Hyundai Motor Company, South Korea, it combines advanced mobility technologies, high localization and sustainable manufacturing; per the BRSR, manufacture of passenger cars accounts for 88.05% of turnover and sale of vehicle parts and accessories 4.92%.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Global economy: growth broadly sustained at around 3.5% in 2025 (IMF July 2026 WEO Update), supported by accommodative financial conditions, policy support and technology-led investment; outlook cautiously moderated, with growth expected to ease to around 3.0% in 2026.
- Global inflation rose from 4.1% in 2025 to around 4.4% in 2026 on West Asia conflict-driven energy and logistics costs; expected to moderate gradually to 3.7% by 2027 assuming easing commodity prices.
- India macro: real GDP growth estimated at 7.7% in FY 26 (PIB) versus 7.1% in FY 25, led by secondary and tertiary sectors each expanding above 9%; IMF projects India real GDP growth of 6.4% for FY 27 and 6.7% for FY 28.
- GST 2.0 rate rationalization (simplified two-slab structure of 5% and 18%) was a key catalyst — described by the CFO as a strong growth catalyst from September that improved affordability and household disposable income; supported by income tax rationalization, multiple repo rate cuts and benign inflation of 2.1% for much of the year.
- Indian auto industry: FY 26 was a milestone year with all major segments recording their highest annual sales in seven years; SIAM total industry production of 34.7 million units.
- Passenger vehicles: record domestic sales of 46,43,439 units in FY 26, +7.9% YoY, with a highest-ever quarterly 13,16,282 units in Q4 on festive demand and improved retail conversions; drivers cited are improved affordability, tax rationalization, lower financing costs and sustained preference for utility vehicles and feature-rich models.
- Electrification: overall EV passenger vehicle growth of 93.9% (EV contribution to PV rising to 3.4% / 157,514 units in FY 26 from 1.9% / 81,226 units in FY 25); electric passenger vehicle registrations grew over 94%. Policy support from PLI-Auto, PLI for ACC battery storage, PM E-DRIVE, PM-eBus Sewa and SPMEPCI.
- Exports as a structural growth lever: India PV (4-wheeler) exports at a record 9,05,200 units, +17.5%, on steady demand from the Middle East, Africa and Latin America.
- Global auto: light vehicle sales of approximately 91.7 million units in 2025, surpassing pre-pandemic levels for the first time; projected at 91.86 million units in 2026 (S&P Global Mobility) — marginal growth, with production expected to moderate in 2026 amid trade policy uncertainty including US automotive tariffs.
- Softening electrification momentum in certain markets on affordability, infrastructure gaps and evolving subsidy regimes, leading to a more balanced shift towards hybrids and alternative powertrains — a driver behind HMIL's hybrid-ready architectures.
- Structural transformation through digitalization and software-defined vehicles, enabling new revenue streams via connected services and over-the-air upgrades.
- Supply chain risk, particularly in semiconductors and critical minerals, remains a key challenge for global manufacturers.
- Company-specific FY 26 drivers per the CFO: commissioning of the Pune plant coincided with the GST-driven demand improvement and the product launch cycle kicking in, collectively supporting HMIL's growth trajectory.
- Export business delivered 21.43% YoY revenue growth (CFO's statement); export destinations increased from over 60 countries in FY 25 to more than 70 countries in FY 26; VERNA and Grand i10 anchored export volumes, with strong demand from Latin America, Africa and Asia-Pacific.
- Mix driver: SUVs contributed ~68% of domestic sales in FY 26, significantly ahead of industry trends, led by CRETA.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: HMIL's expansion story in FY 26 is the operationalisation of the Talegaon (Pune) plant. The facility was acquired from General Motors in August 2023 as a strategic brownfield acquisition, which the Company says let it accelerate capacity expansion through a capital-efficient route while significantly reducing the execution timelines associated with a greenfield project. Over FY 25 and FY 26 the plant underwent extensive revitalization and modernization aligned with Hyundai's latest global manufacturing standards, with the transformation completed within 19 months. Passenger vehicle production commenced in October 2025 and the plant is being ramped up in a phased manner; it currently adds 1,70,000 units to annual production capacity, with a stated total capacity of 3,20,000 units in phases by 2030. The plant is conceptualised as a flexible facility capable of producing both ICE vehicles and EVs on the same production lines, and it incorporates Industry 4.0 technology — advanced robotics across welding, painting and assembly, AI-enabled real-time quality inspection, machine-learning predictive maintenance, IoT-enabled equipment and digitally connected shopfloor systems. Within the first month of operations it transitioned to two-shift production; it recorded zero field complaints in its first 100 days, an exceptionally low warranty claim rate and over 16 million accident-free man-hours, and produced 64,830 units in FY 26 (production, not capacity). Strategically located in western India, Pune strengthens logistics and export capability through proximity to Mumbai ports and the Maharashtra/Gujarat component clusters and diversifies HMIL's manufacturing footprint beyond a single region. The Chennai plant remains the cornerstone of operations with an installed annual capacity of 8,24,000 units, and with Pune added the Company's total installed capacity has reached approximately 1 million units per annum. HMIL currently manufactures 15 passenger vehicle models across 450+ variants through a flexible, integrated manufacturing setup. On the composition of spend, the BRSR (Principle 2, Essential Indicator 1) states that EV-related capex was 4% of total capital expenditure in FY 2025-26 versus 10% in FY 2024-25, described as covering 'EV Cars, Battery Assembly Plant, Plant Expansion, Charging Station', while EV-related R&D was 30% of total R&D in FY 2025-26 versus 38% in FY 2024-25 — i.e. the EV share of the capital programme fell sharply year on year. || NAMED DISCLOSURE DEFECT — capital commitments figures NOT extracted: the '=== NAMED DISCLOSURE — CAPITAL COMMITMENTS ===' block supplied with this bundle carries no readable column dates (the header reads only 'As at | Year ended', with no year against either column) and no unit line (no 'Rs Million / Rs Lakhs / Rs Crore' statement anywhere in the block). Note also that the block prints two DIFFERENT pairs of figures for the same line item from two different pages (page 159 and page 193, presumably standalone and consolidated, though neither is labelled), which is a second reason the rows are not usable as stated. || SCOPE NOTE — the routed 'MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION & ANALYSIS' section of this bundle does not contain MD&A at all; it contains Annexure 'D' CSR impact-assessment write-ups (Art for Hope, clean water in Madhya Pradesh, rural sports, ITI support, Assam disaster management) and contributed no capex or capacity content. strategy.title: Strategy
strategy.body:
- Strategic focus for FY 27 — strengthen the SUV portfolio through the launch of two all-new nameplates: a localized dedicated mass electric SUV and a new ICE SUV.
- Accelerate the transition to electric mobility through localization, charging infrastructure and ecosystem development.
- Deepen digital initiatives to enhance customer convenience across the ownership journey, and expand connected, software-defined and intelligent mobility capabilities for a more seamless and personalized experience.
- Continue to strengthen a future-ready manufacturing ecosystem through sustainability, operational flexibility and localization.
- Enhance export competitiveness through the Chennai and Pune facilities, leveraged as integrated manufacturing and export hubs; Pune added as an export base to improve supply chain resilience and operational flexibility.
- Broaden customer accessibility across urban and emerging markets by further expanding and upgrading the retail and service network (1,508 sales outlets across 1,125 cities and towns; 89 net additions in FY 26 including significant rural expansion).
- Advance eco-friendly powertrains through EVs, CNG and hybrid-ready architectures.
- Enhance energy efficiency and waste reduction across the Chennai and Pune facilities, and strengthen manufacturing processes to support long-term operational sustainability.
- Expand connected-car technologies, software-enabled features and advanced safety systems across the portfolio; deploy connected cockpit ecosystems (navigation, apps, personalization, shared profiles); increase adoption of ADAS and intelligent driver-assistance technologies across models.
- Strengthen the N Line portfolio to address demand for performance-oriented mobility experiences.
- Strengthen dealer capability through Regional Learning Centers, Technical Training Academies and Bodyshop Academies, and enhance EV readiness and digital integration across the dealer ecosystem.
- Build an intelligent service ecosystem through workshop automation, diagnostics and digital integration; expand digital/AI customer touchpoints (myHyundai app with EV Charge section giving access to over 28,000 EV charging points, Smart Pick-up & Drop, Remote Care Program, CRM, AI-enabled virtual assistants and multilingual interfaces).
- Expand the use of AI for marketing and customer engagement — faster content creation, more personalized interactions and intelligent digital platforms that anticipate customer needs.
- 'Make in India, Made for the World' — fortify India's position as a key global export hub within Hyundai Motor Company's worldwide operations, with access to more than 150 markets through Hyundai's global network.
- Pursue product cost competitiveness through R&D-led Value Engineering — strategic planning, master plan preparation, customer-centric optimization and material localization / local sourcing.
- Strengthen manufacturing flexibility, supply chain resilience and export readiness to support future demand.
- The routed text contains no articulated dividend policy or capital-allocation philosophy statement — no payout-ratio target, buyback, debt-reduction plan or credit rating is disclosed anywhere in this bundle. The only concrete capital-allocation action disclosed is in the Notice of the 30th AGM (to be held on Wednesday, August 26, 2026 at 2:00 P.M. hero.oneLiner: Hyundai Motor India Limited (HMIL) is one of India's leading passenger vehicle manufacturers and a key pillar of the Hyundai Group's global growth strategy, anchored in the philosophy of 'Progress for Humanity'.
